iti pakṣaśabdena tadgataṃ sādhanaṃ, pratipakṣaśabdenaca tanniṣṭhaṃ dūṣaṇamiti tatra kā yuktirnāma anyā bhavet | pramāṇasya sā parikara iti tu anayā bhāṣayā śabdaprayojana āvarjyate, na vastupriyaḥ | parikaro hi kāraṇaṃ vā kāryaṃ vā sahakāri vā sahakāryaṃ vā, na punaraparaḥ parikaraḥ kaścit | tasmāt yuktiriti tāvadanumānameveti sāṃkhyādayaḥ | āvītahetubhyo hi vipakṣavyāvṛttiṃ te icchanti | samādhānanairmalyāt- mikā pratibhā iti tu tatrabhavadbhartṛhariprabhṛtayaḥ | tadanusāra evaca ayamamandatvaṃ prajñāyā iti arthāpattiriti mīmāṃsakāḥ | bādhakapramāṇarūpameva anumānaṃ pratyakṣavikalpaparyantībhavadekopalambhānubhavāditinyāyena svasaṃvidi pariniṣṭhitamiti bauddhāḥ | pramāṇayojanātmakaṃ pramātṛsvātantryameva yuktiriti pratyabhijñātattvavit | yatkiñcidapi ca a"gnīkurvatā avaśyameva paryante pramātṛsvātantryameva jñānakriyāśaktiyojanātmakamaṅgīkartavyamiti asakṛduktam | loke'pica upāyayojanameva svātantryotthāpitaṃ yuktiriti prasiddham-yuktyā kuru, yuktyā saṃkaṭāduttīrṇo'smīti | tat tatraiva avadheyaṃ sumatibhiriti atra asmābhirnibandhaḥ kṛtaḥ, natu āhopuruṣikayeti alam | evaṃ tanmātrānubandhitvaṃ yatsvabhāvahetuviṣayasya jīvitaṃ, tatrāpi kāryakāraṇabhāva eva mūlamiti upapādya, ācāryasya etadeva saṃmatamiti upapādayati ata eva taiḥ iti | nanu kimanena uktena bhavadabhimatamuktaṃ bhavati | bhavatītyāha tena iti itiśabdāvamṛṣṭena paṭhitena granthena niraṃśe'pi vastuni tairidamuktaṃ bhavati-yat gamakasyetyādi itiśabdaparāmṛṣṭam | nanu iyatā kiṃ sidhyati | āha evaṃca iti | (page 210) asyāpi iti yasya āpāte kāryakāraṇagarbhatā na ābhāti mandamatīnām, tasyāpi; na kevalaṃ dhūmavattvādagnimattvamityādeḥ | tato'pi iti pūrvameṣa granthaḥ svabhāvahetorviśeṣaṇāya upāttaḥ svabhāvahetuṃ kaṃcideva gamayatītyevaṃ vyākhyātam | adhunā tu sarva eva svabhāvaheturevaṃbhūto veditavya iti paraṃ bodhayituṃ viśeṣaṇaṃ prayuktamiti vyākhyābhedaḥ | evaṃcābhidhānasya phalaṃ kṛpayā asmannaye sopānakrameṇaiva paro'dhirohaṇīyo mohamahāndhakūpāt yena ayaṃ viśrāmyediti vyut
**Inference across knowers, and the mirror of consciousness** We have said that causality is the conscious knower's agency. But this draws a sharp objection from the Buddhist idealist, the Vijñānavādin. "If everything is appearance," he says, "then cause and effect are only relations *between appearances*. An un-manifested fire is nothing at all. So how can the smoke-appearance arise from it? And how can you infer the fire from the smoke?" Abhinavagupta's answer is subtle and rests on the one creation. The Vijñānavādin, holding each conscious stream to have its own private appearances, could find cause and effect only within his own smoke-and-fire appearances — he can never reach another's. But in our view this is wrong. The Lord creates the appearances *for all the knowers at once, as one*. So when we grasp the pervasion — that smoke implies fire — the smoke-appearance and the fire-appearance belong, in the Lord's single creation, to every knower alike. The smoke-appearance arises from the fire-appearance, and this pervasion can be grasped, once, for all. And for the whole range of knowers — from the worm to the omniscient — the fire-appearance is one, not split by the difference of streams; so the smoke can arise from it and from nothing else. That fire-appearance, being indirect to the one who infers, is what we call the "cause of the Lord" (adhipatipratyaya); it is new, not like the smoke that is born of smoke. It is the non-wandering, effect-marker, by which the inference is actually made. So inference holds across knowers, because the Lord has created the appearances as one. Now, the dependence of cause and effect — the "in-this-existing-this-is" that the pervasion expresses. Here Abhinavagupta is careful. The dependence is not a real *otherness* between two separate things. The fire and its heat: their distinction is only constructed. The fire, as the shining own-marker, cannot have the heat as a separate own-form — both are of equal cause, both come from the one reality. So in truth the dependence is one, quickened by the synthesis, by the awareness that joins them. The grammatical point — the locative "in fire [there is] heat" — is not meaningless, nor does it point to a merely fabricated referent; it is real, and it is supported by the one knower. The dependence of cause and effect is not two things leaning on each other; it is one thing known as one. But what if the Sāṃkhya, with its own account of transformation, offers a better story? Here Abhinavagupta shows that even the Sāṃkhya's "dry" cause-and-effect is not dry. The Sāṃkhya says: there is one substance — the seed, or the primal principle — with an ordered variety of natures; the earlier nature is the cause, the later is the effect; the whole evolves by transformation (pariṇāma). But Abhinavagupta's point is that the transformation itself is an *action*. The transition from the earlier nature, given up, to the later nature, newly unfolded, is precisely the agent-act-object structure — the freedom of transforming, which is agency. So even in the Sāṃkhya view, causality is not the dry change of a thing; it already contains the free knower's act. The intellect, the earth, the sprout — all are states of the one substance, and the transformation that runs through them is an action. And finally, the great closing argument — why only *consciousness* can bear difference and non-difference at all. The inert, Abhinavagupta says, is a fixed form. It is a known object, and as a known object it is "different" with respect to another thing (the blue as against the non-blue) and "non-different" with respect to itself. But the *very same* nature cannot be both different and non-different — that is a contradiction. So the inert, being a known object, cannot be many-natured. But consciousness is different. It does not fall into the state of a known object. Like a clear, free mirror, it bears the whole variety of appearances as its *reflections* (pratibimba) — and those ref
